Raw Archive Entry · March 2026

"Woke at 5:30 AM. Read twenty pages of Seneca's Epistles with black coffee. Noticing how much modern productivity advice is just repackaged Stoicism with a subscription fee."

Fragments & Marginalia

  • On Reading Velocity: The greatest delusion is that skimming fifty summaries equals understanding one difficult paragraph. If your eyes aren't stopping, your brain isn't wrestling.

The Multi-Potentialite Advantage

"Specialization is for insects. A human being should be able to write an essay, design a system, critique a film, listen to a frequency, and ship a product."

What I Do for a Living

I am Avdhut Kulkarni, a Senior Product Designer and Systems Thinker. I work at the intersection of human interface design, design system architecture, and engineering velocity.

My work is grounded in:

  1. First-Principles Product Design: Stripping away decorative noise to reveal the fundamental interaction model.
  2. Design Tokens & Systems: Building scalable, maintainable multi-brand systems that allow design and engineering pods to ship in lockstep.
  3. High-Leverage Tooling: Creating tools, SSGs, and workflows that multiply human output without adding bureaucracy.
Input                  Multi-Disciplinary Synthesis               Output
Literature + Cinema + Sound  ──>  Deep Empathy & Rhythm  ──>  Calm, Timeless Products

Selected Case Studies & Inquiries

  • Design Systems at Scale: Unifying 40+ products under an atomic token architecture.
  • Developer Experience Engine: Reducing build friction and handoff latency by 70%.

Let's make something timeless together.

title: The Stormlight Archive: Kaladin and the Weight of Protection
subtitle: Why Bridge Four's philosophy of holding the bridge echoes the highest Stoic duty
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: Life before death. Strength before weakness. Journey before destination. — The First Ideal
excerpt: In Brandon Sanderson's epic, Kaladin Stormblessed begins as a broken slave carrying heavy wooden bridges across chasms. His transcendence is not through power, but through duty.
cardSnippet: You cannot protect others if you despise yourself. The First Ideal is not a slogan; it is an operating system for carrying suffering.
htmlContent:
The First Ideal of the Knights Radiant

"Life before death. Strength before weakness. Journey before destination."

The Tragedy of the Bridge Crew

In The Way of Kings, Brandon Sanderson presents one of the most harrowing situations in modern fantasy: Bridge Four. Men condemned to carry immense timbers across chasms under raining arrows from the Parshendi, serving solely as disposable meat shields for Highprince Sadeas.

Most men broken by such circumstances succumb to despair. Kaladin does something far harder: he refuses apathy.

He gathers sap, disinfects arrow wounds with knobweed, teaches pariahs how to stand together, and transforms a death squad into a brotherhood.

The Windrunner's Paradox

The core struggle of Kaladin Stormblessed is the burden of the protector:

  • How do you protect those who cannot protect themselves?
  • How do you accept that you cannot save everyone?

The Fourth Ideal is perhaps the most devastating and therapeutic sentence in fantasy literature:

The Fourth Ideal

"I accept that there will be those I cannot protect."

Marcus Aurelius would have recognized Kaladin immediately. Both were men forced into leadership across bloody frontlines, carrying a perpetual war within their own chests. The courage is not in the absence of depression, but in stepping forward anyway.

title: Mistborn: The Final Empire and the Secret in the Mists
subtitle: Kelsier's defiant smile and Vin's journey from survival to trust
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: There's always another secret. — Kelsier, Survivor of Hathsin
excerpt: A thousand years of ash falling from the sky. Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn reimagines rebellion not as a battle of armies, but as a daring heist of faith and steel.
cardSnippet: To smile in the face of a totalitarian god is the ultimate rebellion. Kelsier weaponized hope like an allomantic metal.
htmlContent:
The Survivor's Axiom

"There's always another secret. Smile, Vin. Laughter is the one thing the Lord Ruler cannot take from us."

Ash Falling from the Sky

Mistborn: The Final Empire opens in a world where the prophesied hero failed a millennium ago. The ash falls perpetually from red skies; plants are brown; the Skaa are enslaved beneath the immortal iron fist of the Lord Ruler.

In this suffocating dystopia, Kelsier does not simply plot assassination. He orchestrates a myth.

Vin: The Traumatized Street Urchin

While Kelsier is the flamboyant architect of rebellion, Vin is the emotional anchor of the trilogy:

  • Beaten and betrayed by her brother Reen, her instinct is radical isolation: anyone who loves you will eventually sell you out.
  • Over three books, Vin’s greatest superpower is not burning pewter, brass, or duralumin—it is learning to trust Elend and her crew.

Allomancy is brilliant kinetic physics, but Sanderson’s real magic is human redemption.

title: Red Rising: The Rage of Lykos and the Cost of Liberty
subtitle: How Darrow of Lykos weaponized myth to dismantle a gilded solar empire
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: I would have lived in peace. But my enemies brought me war. — Darrow of Lykos
excerpt: Pierce Brown's Red Rising is Homeric Greek tragedy injected into the cold vacuum of the solar system. Darrow does not fight for power; he fights for Eo's song.
cardSnippet: The measure of a man is not how much he suffers, but how much suffering he can transmute into freedom for others.
htmlContent:
The Reaper's Declaration

"I would have lived in peace. But my enemies brought me war."

The Blood and Soil of Mars

Red Rising begins in the suffocating helium-3 mines of Mars. Darrow is a Helldiver, convinced by the propaganda of the Society that Reds are sacrificing themselves to pioneer the terraforming of the Red Planet.

When he discovers that humanity has already inhabited Mars for centuries in opulent, decadent floating cities, the lie detonates.

The SlingBlade Philosophy

Darrow's journey into the Institute—carved into a Gold, adopting their aristocratic dialect, and wielding their curved razors—is a masterclass in asymmetrical warfare:

  1. Never play by their rules: When the Golds expect classical duels, Darrow flips the chessboard.
  2. Loyalty forged in blood: Sevro, Cassius, Mustang, and Ragnar become brothers and sisters not through bloodline, but through shared sacrifice.
  3. The cost of revolution: You cannot break a system built on three centuries of slavery without bleeding on your own hands.
The Howler Motto

"Omnis vir lupus" — Everyone is a wolf. Find your pack and hold the line.

title: The Lord of the Rings: Gandalf and the Stewardship of Time
subtitle: Pity, perseverance, and why the smallest hobbit alters the course of Middle-earth
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us. — Gandalf
excerpt: Tolkien's legendarium is not a escapist distraction; it is a profound Catholic and pagan meditation on grief, temptation, and unexpected grace.
cardSnippet: Despair is only for those who see the end beyond all doubt. We do not. Keep walking even through Moria's dark.
htmlContent:
Gandalf to Frodo in the Mines of Moria

"So do all who live to see such times. But that is not for them to decide. All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us."

Pity over Might

In The Lord of the Rings, the ultimate defeat of Sauron does not come from a grand confrontation between archmages or kings.

  • It was Bilbo’s pity in sparing Gollum in The Hobbit that preserved the thread of providence.
  • It was Frodo’s quiet endurance across the ash heaps of Gorgoroth.
  • It was Samwise Gamgee holding his master’s hand when water ran dry.

The Bibliophile's North Star

Whenever modern life feels overwhelming with algorithmic noise and manufactured crises, return to Tolkien. 

Power Corrupts          -> The One Ring
True Strength           -> Humility & Fellowship
The Cure for Despair    -> Doing the next small duty
Sam's Epiphany

"There's some good in this world, Mr. Frodo... and it's worth fighting for."

title: The Architecture of Specific Knowledge
subtitle: Why you cannot be trained for what makes you genuinely irreplaceable
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "Specific knowledge cannot be taught, but it can be learned. — Naval Ravikant"
excerpt: Specific knowledge is found much more by pursuing your innate curiosity than by chasing whatever is trending.
cardSnippet: Society trains people for jobs that can be outsourced. Cultivate what feels like play to you but looks like work to others.
htmlContent:
Naval's Axiom

"Specific knowledge is found by pursuing your genuine curiosity and passion rather than whatever is hot right now. If you're not 100% into it, somebody else who is 100% into it will outperform you."

The Mirage of Transferable Credentials

In modern academic and corporate life, we are trained to seek transferable credentials: standardized degrees, certifications, and universal checklists. But anything that can be taught in a curriculum can also be outsourced, automated, or taught to a million competitors.

Specific knowledge is different. It is found much more by pursuing your innate curiosity and obsession than by asking: what does the market want right now?

When you pursue what feels like play to you, but looks like work to others, you create a natural moat. Nobody can compete with you on being you.

The Three Hallmarks of Specific Knowledge

  1. It is acquired through apprenticeship and curiosity, not classroom lectures. You cannot read a textbook to learn judgment in chaotic environments. You learn it by making bets, taking scars, and watching masters at work.
  2. It often appears weird or trivial at first. Think of early computer hobbyists tinkering in garages in 1975, or obsessively cataloging obscure Latin translations in a monastery. What the world later discovers as immense leverage often begins as a solitary obsession.
  3. It operates with high accountability. You cannot have specific knowledge without putting your name on the line. When you take accountability, you take the downside risks, but you gain the upside of equity and reputation.
Marginal Note from Obsidian

Compare this with permissionless leverage and the judgment trade. When specific knowledge meets scalable code and media, output is disconnected from input.

The Test of Play vs. Work

Ask yourself:

  • What did you do between ages 12 and 18 when nobody told you what to study?
  • What books do you read that you never feel compelled to skim?
  • What problem keeps you awake not out of anxiety, but out of fascination?

Specific knowledge cannot be taught, but it can be learned. If they can train you for it, they will eventually train an AI or hire someone at half the price to replace you. Guard your eccentricities.

title: Oppenheimer (2023): Fire, Theory, and the Terror of Chain Reactions
subtitle: Christopher Nolan's 70mm chamber drama disguised as a blockbuster
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: They won't fear it until they understand it, and they won't understand it until they've used it.
excerpt:
[!quote] The Trinity Test
 "We knew the world would not be the same. A few people laughed, a few people cried, most people were silent." — J. Robert Oppenhe...
cardSnippet:
[!quote] The Trinity Test
 "We knew the world would not be the same. A few people laughed, a few people cried, most...
logline: The story of American scientist J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in the development of the atomic bomb.
htmlContent:
The Trinity Test

"We knew the world would not be the same. A few people laughed, a few people cried, most people were silent." — J. Robert Oppenheimer

A Symphony of Fission and Conscience

Christopher Nolan does not film Oppenheimer as a celebratory military triumph. He films it as a horror film of ideas.

From the opening frames of rain ripples colliding in puddles to the violent quantum flashes behind Cillian Murphy’s hollow blue eyes, the film is about one terrifying realization: a chain reaction once started cannot be contained.

The Trinity Sequence

The Trinity explosion is legendary cinema not for bombastic noise, but for total silence. Nolan withholds the sound wave for nearly two agonizing minutes. We watch the incandescent fireball blossom in total vacuum—silent, pure, demonic beauty—until the physical shockwave hits the bunker and rattles the theater floor.

The Foot-Stamping Gym Speech

The true climax of the film is not Trinity; it is the gymnasium victory speech. As Oppenheimer gives patriotic platitudes to a roaring crowd, the audio distorts into screaming wind, a blinding white flash washes out the faces, and he steps over the charred ash of his own conscience.

Technical Note

Shot on Kodak 65mm and IMAX black-and-white analog stock. Hoyte van Hoytema’s close-up lensing turns the human face into a landscape as vast as the New Mexico desert.

title: Radiohead — In Rainbows (2007): The Analog Warmth of Disconnection
subtitle: Tape compression, fingerpicked arpeggios, and why 15 Step redefined modern mixing
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: Because we separate like ripples on a blank shore... In rainbows.
excerpt:
[!quote] Thom Yorke on Reckoner
 "An entire song anchored by a single cymbal crash and a golden string arrangement."

 The Masterpiece of Dynamic Range

I...
cardSnippet:
[!quote] Thom Yorke on Reckoner
 "An entire song anchored by a single cymbal crash and a golden string arrangement."...
htmlContent:
Thom Yorke on Reckoner

"An entire song anchored by a single cymbal crash and a golden string arrangement."

The Masterpiece of Dynamic Range

In 2007, during the absolute nadir of the "Loudness Wars" where commercial pop CDs were brickwalled into distorted dynamic sludge, Radiohead and producer Nigel Godrich went in the exact opposite direction.

In Rainbows is celebrated by sound engineers not just for its songcraft, but for its infinite acoustic breathing room:

1. The Clapping Polymeter of 15 Step

The track kicks off with a sharp 5/4 drum machine glitch loop recorded through an analog filter, accompanied by children cheering recorded at a London school, and Colin Greenwood’s warm, rounded bass line that anchors the entire groove.

2. The Holographic Soundstage of Weird Fishes/Arpeggi

Listen on open-back planar magnetic headphones or high-sensitivity studio monitors:

  • Ed O’Brien and Jonny Greenwood’s interlocking Stratocasters pan symmetrically left and right.
  • Phil Selway’s ghost notes on the snare dance like ripples on calm water.
  • You can hear the physical wood resonance of the acoustic instruments.
Listening Setup

Best experienced on analog vinyl or 24-bit/96kHz lossless FLAC. Dim the room lights and listen through uninterrupted.

title: Blade Runner 2049 (2017): The Miracle of an Manufactured Soul
subtitle: Denis Villeneuve and Roger Deakins construct cinema's loneliest masterpiece
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: Dying for the right cause. It's the most human thing we can do.
excerpt:
[!quote] K's Realization
 "I have memories, but they're not real. They're just someone else's."

 The Brutalist Melancholy of K

Sequels arrived 35 years...
cardSnippet:
[!quote] K's Realization
 "I have memories, but they're not real. They're just someone else's."

 The Brutalist Me...
logline: Young Blade Runner K's discovery of a long-buried secret leads him to track down former Blade Runner Rick Deckard.
htmlContent:
K's Realization

"I have memories, but they're not real. They're just someone else's."

The Brutalist Melancholy of K

Sequels arrived 35 years late are supposed to be nostalgic commercial cash grabs. Blade Runner 2049 is instead an existential prayer.

Ryan Gosling’s Officer K is the most heartbreaking protagonist in modern science fiction:

  • He is programmed to obey.
  • He endures baseline calibration tests designed to measure if he feels too much grief.
  • When he begins to hope that he might be the miracle child—born, not made—the film allows him that glimmer of dignity.

And then Villeneuve rips the rug away: K is not the chosen one. He is simply another cog in the machine.

The Climax in the Snow

Yet in discovering he is not the chosen one, K achieves genuine free will. Choosing to save Deckard and die quietly on the snow-covered steps while Hans Zimmer and Benjamin Wallfisch's Tears in the Rain reprise swells is the purest definition of humanity:

The Final Stanza

“Dying for the right cause is the most human thing we can do.”

He doesn’t need a soul given to him by a manufacturer. He forged one with his own choices.

title: The Bibliophile's Guide to Reading and Forgetting
subtitle: You do not remember the meals that kept you alive, yet they formed your bones
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "I cannot remember the books I've read any more than the meals I have eaten; even so, they have made me. — Ralph Waldo Emerson"
excerpt: Reading is not a competitive race to count volumes on Goodreads. It is conversation across centuries with departed minds.
cardSnippet: Stop finishing bad books. The opportunity cost of a mediocre page is a masterpiece left unopened.
htmlContent:
Emerson's Observation

"I cannot remember the books I've read any more than the meals I have eaten; even so, they have made me."

The Vanity of the Reading Goal

Every January, intelligent people set an arbitrary number: I will read 52 books this year.

This metric rewards brevity, shallowness, and speed-reading over deep comprehension. If you read 52 airport business books, you have absorbed roughly twelve recycled tweets padded into 250 pages each.

If instead you spent an entire year wrestling with The Enchiridion of Epictetus, Montaigne's Essays, and Jorge Luis Borges' Ficciones, your year would be infinitely richer.

How to Read Like a Bibliophile

1. Ruthless Abandonment

The moment a book bores you after page thirty, shut it. Put it down without guilt. Life is too short and there are too many magnificent books written over three thousand years to waste time on bad prose.

2. Reread the Top 1%

The best books are not meant to be read once; they are meant to be lived with.

  • When you reread a book at 20, 30, and 40, the book hasn't changed—you have.
  • Naval says: "I would rather read the best 100 books over and over again until I absorb them completely than read all the books."

3. Read with a Pen in Hand

A book that is clean is a book that was merely visited, not inhabited. Underline, write marginalia in the gutters, argue with the author in pencil. Turn the physical artifact into a dialog between two minds.

Obsidian Workflow Note

When an idea hits you while reading, don't summarize the chapter. Capture your own reaction in your vault. Link it to marginalia on borges and books that shaped my mind.

The Ultimate Filter

Read what you love until you love to read. Then read the originals, not the commentary on the originals.

title: Midnight Marginalia: The Paradox of the Creative Night
subtitle: Why the quietest hours between 1 AM and 4 AM belong entirely to the maker
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: In the night all cats are grey, but all ideas are luminous.
excerpt: The telephone is dead; Slack is asleep; the algorithms have stopped chirping. Midnight is when original thought finally breathes.
cardSnippet:
[!note] Midnight Log
 "The world is asleep. There are no notifications to respond to, no peer expectations, no meeti...
htmlContent:
Midnight Log

"The world is asleep. There are no notifications to respond to, no peer expectations, no meetings. In this brief pocket of time, you are entirely free."

The Solitude Dividend

Why do bibliophiles and makers love late hours? It is not about sleep deprivation; it is about psychological insulation. When society powers down, the atmospheric pressure of other people's anxieties lifts. You can sit with a book, a sketch, or a musical passage and exist purely in the moment.

title: Dune: Part Two (2024): The Descent of the False Messiah
subtitle: Denis Villeneuve captures the terror of Frank Herbert's anti-hero warning
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: Lead them to Paradise... May thy knife chip and shatter.
excerpt:
[!quote] The Prophecy of Arrakis
 "He who can destroy a thing has the real control of it." — Paul Atreides

 Cinema as Ancient Religious Myth

Where most...
cardSnippet:
[!quote] The Prophecy of Arrakis
 "He who can destroy a thing has the real control of it." — Paul Atreides

 Cinem...
logline: Paul Atreides unites with Chani and the Fremen while seeking revenge against the conspirators who destroyed his family.
htmlContent:
The Prophecy of Arrakis

"He who can destroy a thing has the real control of it." — Paul Atreides

Cinema as Ancient Religious Myth

Where most sci-fi blockbusters celebrate the hero’s ascension, Frank Herbert and Denis Villeneuve subvert it completely. Dune: Part Two is not the triumph of a savior; it is the birth of a galactic holy war that will kill billions.

Timothée Chalamet's transition from grieving boy in the rocks to the terrifying, commanding voice of Muad'Dib shouting down the Great Houses in the war council is spine-chilling.

The Black Sun of Giedi Prime

The monochromatic infrared sequence on Giedi Prime—Feyd-Rautha’s gladiatorial arena filmed with special infrared cameras—strips color from the spectrum and reveals the Harkonnens as pure photographic parasites.

Sound Design

Hans Zimmer replaces orchestral strings with bagpipes, gut-rumbling thumper frequencies, and synthesized war cries. This isn’t background music; it is physical weather.

title: Hans Zimmer — Interstellar (2014): The Breath of the Temple Organ
subtitle: How four-stop church pipes and ticking watches captured cosmic time dilation
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: Time is a resource. A luxury. And every tick of the clock is another day lost.
excerpt:
[!quote] Christopher Nolan's Brief to Zimmer
 "I gave Hans an envelope with one piece of paper containing a fable about a father having to leave his child....
cardSnippet:
[!quote] Christopher Nolan's Brief to Zimmer
 "I gave Hans an envelope with one piece of paper containing a fable ab...
htmlContent:
Christopher Nolan's Brief to Zimmer

"I gave Hans an envelope with one piece of paper containing a fable about a father having to leave his child. I never told him it was science fiction."

The Physicality of Temple Church

To record the score, Hans Zimmer bypassed Hollywood scoring stages and moved his team to Temple Church in London, built in the 12th century by the Knights Templar.

The centerpiece is the 1927 Harrison & Harrison four-manual pipe organ:

  • The low pedal notes vibrate at 16 Hz to 32 Hz—sub-bass frequencies that human ears cannot hear directly, but which vibrate inside the human ribcage.
  • The sound of the organist pumping air into the bellows was left deliberately in the mix, giving the instrument the sound of an astronaut breathing inside a helmet.

Mountains and the 1.25-Second Metric

In the track Mountains, each audible tick is spaced at 1.25 seconds. On Miller’s water planet, every tick represents an entire day passing on Earth.

Acoustic Spatialization

The vast cathedral reverberation creates an acoustic cathedral of stars. A benchmark test for subwoofer bass extension and soundstage depth.

title: The Judgment Trade
subtitle: In an age of infinite leverage, one good decision outweighs ten thousand hours of brute labor
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "If you want to be rich, you need to understand that judgment is worth far more than effort. — Naval Ravikant"
excerpt: A runner who sprints frantically in the wrong direction loses to someone who strolls deliberately toward the summit.
cardSnippet: In modern work, 99% of effort is wasted without direction. Direction is judgment. Judgment comes from calm and experience.
htmlContent:
Naval on Direction

"The direction you are heading in matters more than how fast you are moving. Most people spend their entire lives sprinting blindly on the treadmill."

Effort vs. Judgment

In an industrial economy, labor was linear. If you spent ten hours turning bolts on an assembly line, you produced roughly twice as much as five hours.

In an algorithmic, connected world, leverage is nonlinear.

  • A trader who makes one right macro call creates millions of dollars in seconds.
  • A designer who picks the right system architecture saves three years of technical debt.
  • A writer who crystallizes an evergreen idea reaches millions without expending extra ink.

brute effort has been commoditized. Judgment is scarce.

Where Judgment Originates

Where does genuine judgment come from? It does not come from rushing or panic. It comes from:

  1. Clear thinking without ego. When you don't care about looking smart, you see things as they actually are.
  2. First principles thinking. Deconstruct problems into their most fundamental truths and reason upward from there.
  3. Deep domain intuition through immersion. Reading broadly across physics, mathematics, history, and literature gives you a lattice of mental models.
See also

Explore the subtraction heuristic and calm mind clear thinking for how reducing noise amplifies judgment.

title: Past Lives (2023): In-Yun, The Ferry, and The Weight of Unlived Lives
subtitle: Celine Song's quiet miracle on the geometry of longing
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: If two people get married, they say it’s because their In-Yun has eighty thousand layers of past lives.
excerpt:
[!quote] The Philosophy of In-Yun
 "There is a word in Korean: In-Yun. It means providence or fate. It’s an In-Yun if even two strangers just walk by each o...
cardSnippet:
[!quote] The Philosophy of In-Yun
 "There is a word in Korean: In-Yun. It means providence or fate. It’s an In-Yun i...
logline: Nora and Hae Sung, two deeply connected childhood friends, are wrested apart after Nora's family emigrates from South Korea.
htmlContent:
The Philosophy of In-Yun

"There is a word in Korean: In-Yun. It means providence or fate. It’s an In-Yun if even two strangers just walk by each other in the street and their clothes accidentally brush."

The Quiet Dignity of Adult Love

In almost any Hollywood romance, the arrival of Hae Sung in New York City would lead to cheap melodrama: a jealous husband, a screaming argument in a bar, a dramatic kiss in the torrential rain.

Celine Song rejects every cliché.

Arthur (John Magaro), the Jewish American writer married to Nora, is not an obstacle to be overcome. He is kind, perceptive, and heartbreakingly honest about his insecurities: "You make the world so much bigger and I'm wondering if I'm just the guy you met because you were living in this place."

The Final Walk to the Uber

The film lives or dies in its final three minutes:

  • Nora walks Hae Sung to the street corner.
  • They stand in silence for two full minutes while traffic glides by.
  • Hae Sung looks at her: "See you then."
  • Nora walks back up the apartment steps, collapses into Arthur’s arms, and weeps for the girl she left in Seoul twenty-four years ago.

A masterpiece of restraint and mature emotional truth.

title: Case Study: Scaling an Atomic Token System Across 40+ Products
subtitle: How unifying design tokens reduced developer handoff latency by 65%
author: Avdhut Kulkarni
quote: A design system is not a UI library; it is a shared language between human intent and machine execution.
excerpt: How redesigning the core token pipeline eliminated 120 recurring handoff bugs and aligned three cross-functional squads.
cardSnippet:
[!quote] The Problem
 "Designers were exporting hex codes; engineers were hardcoding pixel margins; every product re...
htmlContent:
The Problem

"Designers were exporting hex codes; engineers were hardcoding pixel margins; every product release introduced subtle, unmeasured visual drift."

The Architectural Solution

We architected a semantic, multi-tiered token architecture:

  1. Global Palette Tokens: Immutable base values (e.g. color.amber.500).
  2. Semantic Context Tokens: Intent-driven variables (e.g. surface.interactive.default, text.editorial.title).
  3. Component-Scoped Tokens: Tightly bound properties that allow automated theme switching between dark, light, and high-contrast modes.

Measurable Results

  • Handoff time reduced by 65% across 3 engineering squads.
  • Zero visual drift across 40+ production components.
  • Automated CI pipeline linking Figma Variables directly to GitHub pull requests.

title: Permissionless Leverage: Code, Media, & The Gutenberg Engine
subtitle: The new aristocrats are those who build armies that work for them while they sleep
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "Code and media are permissionless leverage. They're the leverage behind the newly rich. You can create software and media that works for you while you sleep. — Naval"
excerpt: Humans spent millennia needing someone else's approval to build an empire. Today, a text editor and a keyboard is all that stands between you and infinite reproduction.
cardSnippet: Labor requires human permission. Capital requires bank permission. Code and words require only curiosity and an internet socket.
htmlContent:
The Evolution of Leverage

"Forget rich versus poor, white-collar versus blue-collar. It's now leveraged versus unleveraged."

The Four Forms of Leverage

To understand how value is captured in the modern world, consider the four archetypes of leverage:

1. Labor (Oldest, Hardest)

Having other humans work for you. It requires tremendous politics, management overhead, and emotional friction. Everyone is trying to manage everyone else.

2. Capital (The 20th Century Engine)

Money working for money. It scales well, but requires permission from banks, venture funds, or inherited wealth.

3. Code (The Software Era)

Programs executing instructions round the clock without fatigue. An algorithm will run at 3 AM with zero salary and zero resentment.

4. Media & Writing (The Gutenberg Era Perfected)

Essays, podcasts, books, websites, and recordings. A note written in Obsidian and published to GitHub Pages can be read by 10,000 people simultaneously across six continents while you are asleep in bed.

       Permission Required?        Marginal Cost of Replication
Labor         YES                               HIGH
Capital       YES                               MEDIUM
Code          NO (Permissionless)               ZERO
Media         NO (Permissionless)               ZERO

The Bibliophile's Advantage

When you combine deep reading with writing in public, you are creating permanent intellectual equity. A well-crafted essay does not spoil. It compounds like a high-yield bond.

Connection

See specific knowledge on why genuine curiosity is the compass for permissionless leverage.

title: Marginalia on Borges and the Infinite Library
subtitle: On hexagons, mirrors, labyrinths, and the terror of every possible book
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "I have always imagined that Paradise will be a kind of library. — Jorge Luis Borges"
excerpt: In The Library of Babel, every permutation of letters exists somewhere. The problem is not lack of truth; it is drowning in infinite noise.
cardSnippet: The tragedy of the infinite library is not that truth is missing, but that it is buried under septillions of pages of gibberish.
htmlContent:
Borges' Paradise

"I have always imagined that Paradise will be a kind of library."

The Hexagonal Universe

In The Library of Babel, Jorge Luis Borges constructs a universe composed of an indefinite, perhaps infinite number of hexagonal galleries. In each hexagon there are shelves; on each shelf are thirty-two books of uniform size; each book has four hundred and ten pages; each page, forty lines; each line, eighty letters.

Because the library contains every possible permutation of the alphabet, it holds everything:

  • The detailed history of the future.
  • The lost tragedies of Aeschylus.
  • The accurate translation of every dead language.
  • The true story of your own death.

And along with those, millions of volumes of pure nonsensical clutter: lines like “dhcmrlchtdj” repeating for five hundred leaves.

The Modern Internet as the Library of Babel

We now live inside Borges' library. The internet is that exact infinite hexagon. Every theory, every opinion, every contradictory gospel is accessible in a microsecond.

The challenge of our era is no longer finding information. It is curation, discernment, and subtraction.

When every book is available, the true art is choosing which five to keep on your bedside table.

In Dialogue With

Linked with the subtraction heuristic and reading and retention.

title: Via Negativa: The Subtraction Heuristic
subtitle: True wisdom is not about what you add to your life, but what you systematically remove
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "To get rich, add to your capital. To get happy, subtract from your desires. — Naval Ravikant"
excerpt: We are addicted to additive solutions: more apps, more books, more meetings. Yet the greatest leaps come from elimination.
cardSnippet: Perfection is attained not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away.
htmlContent:
The Ancient Maxim

"Perfection is achieved, not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away." — Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

The Bias Toward Addition

When human beings encounter friction, our default instinct is additive:

  • If we feel unfocused, we download another productivity application.
  • If a project is late, we hire more engineers.
  • If our writing is weak, we add adjectives and complex jargon.

In almost all complex domains, addition increases fragility.

The Power of Via Negativa

Nassim Taleb popularized the concept of Via Negativa (by way of denial or subtraction):

  1. In health: Removing sugar, seed oils, and chronic sleep deprivation produces ten times more vitality than adding twenty exotic supplements.
  2. In writing: Pruning superfluous words and passive voice strengthens an argument far more than embellishment.
  3. In thinking: Avoiding stupidity is far easier than trying to be brilliant. As Charlie Munger said, "It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent."
Addiction to Addition  -> Fragility, Noise, Overhead
Discipline of Subtraction -> Antifragility, Signal, Peace
Practical Exercise

Write a "Not-To-Do" list every Monday morning. What three obligations will you refuse this week?

title: Stoic Equations of Peace: Aurelius at Midnight
subtitle: Meditations from the imperial tent on why nothing external can touch your inner citadel
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "You have power over your mind - not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength. — Marcus Aurelius"
excerpt: When Marcus Aurelius wrote his private notebook at the edge of the Danubian frontier, he was not writing for the Roman senate. He was talking himself down from rage.
cardSnippet: The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.
htmlContent:
The Emperor's Reminder to Himself

"When you wake up in the morning, tell yourself: The people I deal with today will be meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, dishonest, jealous, and surly. They are like this because they cannot distinguish good from evil. But I have seen the beauty of good, and the ugliness of evil..."

The Private Notebook of the Master of the World

Consider who Marcus Aurelius was: the supreme emperor of the Mediterranean world. He had absolute authority over legions, treasuries, and human lives. Yet in the freezing dark of his military camp along the Danube, fighting off plagues and Germanic invasions, he did not write decrees of conquest.

He wrote a therapeutic journal to himself. He never meant for Meditations to be published.

Three Stoic Equations

1. Suffering = Event × Resistance

The external event (the rainstorm, the insulting colleague, the market downturn) is neutral nature. The suffering is your internal judgment: This should not be happening to me.

2. Desire = A Contract You Make to Be Unhappy

Naval Ravikant phrased this with modern precision: "Desire is a contract you make with yourself to be unhappy until you get what you want." Pick at most one desire at a time; otherwise, you scatter your peace.

3. Freedom = Independence from the Opinions of Fools

Why do we love ourselves more than other people, but care more about their opinions than our own? When you stop seeking applause, you cannot be blackmailed.

Internal Thread

Connects with calm mind clear thinking and the judgment trade.

title: The Ten Books That Rewired My Mental Software
subtitle: An annotated canon for the modern autodidact and bibliophile
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "In a world of infinite books, reading the foundational 100 repeatedly is a superpower. — Avadh Kulkarni"
excerpt: If you read the same books everyone else is reading, you will think the same thoughts everyone else is thinking. Here is my foundational shelf.
cardSnippet: A curated library is not furniture; it is an external hard drive for your consciousness.
htmlContent:
Naval on Foundations

"Read science, math, and philosophy one hour a day. That will put you at the upper echelon of human success within seven years."

The Foundational Shelf

Here are the ten works I return to when the noise of modern life threatens to dissolve critical thought:

1. The Almanack of Naval Ravikant — Eric Jorgenson

The definitive handbook on wealth, judgment, leverage, and unconditional happiness. It reads like contemporary Marcus Aurelius mixed with Silicon Valley game theory.

2. Meditations — Marcus Aurelius (Gregory Hays translation)

The ultimate armor against anxiety and status anxiety. Read a single paragraph each evening.

3. Poor Charlie’s Almanack — Charlie Munger & Peter Kaufman

The masterclass on worldly wisdom, multi-disciplinary thinking, and psychological misjudgments.

4. Antifragile — Nassim Nicholas Taleb

Things that gain from disorder. Essential for understanding risk, asymmetry, and modern fragility.

5. Ficciones — Jorge Luis Borges

Labyrinths, infinite libraries, and the paradox of time. Expands the architectural limits of human imagination.

6. The Beginning of Infinity — David Deutsch

A physicist's defense of human explanation and open-ended progress. The best antidote to contemporary cynicism.

7. Essays — Michel de Montaigne

The birth of honest introspection. Montaigne wrote candidly about his flaws, his kidney stones, and his love of quiet books.

8. Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance — Robert Pirsig

An inquiry into Quality and the reconciliation of classical rationality with romantic intuition.

9. Letters from a Stoic — Seneca

Timeless advice on friendship, time management, and the brevity of life.

10. Gödel, Escher, Bach — Douglas Hofstadter

A golden braid connecting formal logic, recursive fugues, and the mystery of consciousness.

Rereading Axiom

If a book isn't worth rereading, it wasn't worth reading once.

title: Calm Mind, Clear Thinking: The Engine of Pure Signal
subtitle: A frantic mind creates frantic solutions; stillness is the ultimate competitive advantage
author: Avadh Kulkarni
quote: "A calm mind, a fit body, and a house full of love. These things cannot be bought. They must be earned. — Naval Ravikant"
excerpt: In a hyper-connected society where everyone is outraged and reactive, the person who can sit quietly in a room for two hours thinking clearly is unstoppable.
cardSnippet: Pascal wrote that all of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone.
htmlContent:
Pascal's Warning

"All of humanity's problems stem from man's inability to sit quietly in a room alone." — Blaise Pascal

The Anxiety Tax

Modern digital culture levies an unacknowledged tax on every thought: The Anxiety Tax.

When your dopamine receptors are perpetually fried by notifications, feeds, and breaking news headlines, you lose the ability to hold a complex thought for more than twenty seconds. You become a reactionary creature, bouncing between micro-stimuli.

How Stillness Multiplies Output

  1. You stop chasing foolish games. Status games are zero-sum. Wealth and knowledge creation are positive-sum. When you are calm, you stop caring about who got promoted to what junior title.
  2. You notice second-order consequences. A stressed thinker only sees the immediate reaction (Order 1). A calm thinker sees what happens after that (Order 2 and 3).
  3. Your judgment becomes decisive. When you aren't agitated, you can say "No" to 99 mediocre invitations so you have the boundless energy to say "Yes" to the singular life-changing opportunity.
The Almanac Principle

"Peace is happiness at rest; happiness is peace in motion." Maintain the sanctuary of your workroom.
